That guidance has changed. Modern browsers (Chrome, Safari) now auto-upgrade every HTTP navigation to HTTPS regardless of any HSTS policy, so preloading only helps in the narrow case where that upgrade fails against an active attacker. The list operator now states it plainly: "**HSTS preloading is not recommended.**" The commitment, meanwhile, is heavy — removal from the list takes months and applies to every subdomain. For nearly all sites, a strong `max-age` with `includeSubDomains` is the right stopping point; skip `preload`.

## Common mistakes

- **Sending HSTS over HTTP.** Browsers must ignore it. Send it on HTTPS responses only.
- **Setting `includeSubDomains` without auditing subdomains.** Every subdomain — including internal tools, staging, and legacy services — must work over HTTPS. If `dev.example.com` is HTTP-only, you have just broken it.
- **Setting `max-age=0` by accident.** That removes HSTS. Useful when rolling back, dangerous when copied from a tutorial.
- **Adding `preload` reflexively.** The preload list is now discouraged by its own operator, and getting a domain off it takes months. Ship HSTS without it unless you have a specific reason.

## Verification

- `curl -sI https://example.com | grep -i strict-transport-security` should return the header.
- In Chrome DevTools, the Security panel shows the HSTS state for the current site.

HSTS is a commitment, not a switch. Plan the rollback path before you ship.

Found 3 results for "INP Interaction to Next Paint":

1. Avoid automatic IP-based language redirects — avoid · i18n
   Automatically redirecting visitors to a locale based on IP geolocation or Accept-Language is an anti-pattern. It traps users in the wrong language, breaks search crawlers, and breaks shared links. Let users choose.
   https://specification.website/spec/i18n/avoid-auto-geo-redirects/
2. Storage Access API — optional · privacy
   As browsers partition and block third-party cookies, embedded cross-site content uses the Storage Access API to request its own cookies behind a user gesture — instead of asking visitors to switch off tracking protection.
   https://specification.website/spec/privacy/storage-access-api/
3. Visible focus indicators — required · accessibility
   Whenever a control receives keyboard focus, the page must show a clear, high-contrast indicator. Removing focus outlines without a replacement is a top accessibility failure.
   https://specification.website/spec/accessibility/focus-indicators/

calls.name: search_spec
calls.result:
Found 5 results for "Core Web Vitals responsiveness":

1. Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS) — required · performance
   Core Web Vitals measure loading, responsiveness, and visual stability. Hit LCP ≤ 2.5s, INP ≤ 200ms, and CLS ≤ 0.1 at the 75th percentile of real users.
   https://specification.website/spec/performance/core-web-vitals/
2. /.well-known/webauthn — optional · well-known
   A JSON document at /.well-known/webauthn lists the origins allowed to use passkeys scoped to a single Relying Party ID. It enables WebAuthn Related Origin Requests — one passkey shared across several domains you own. Only applicable if the site uses passkeys across more than one origin.
   https://specification.website/spec/well-known/webauthn/
3. /.well-known/webfinger — optional · well-known
   WebFinger (RFC 7033) resolves an account identifier such as acct:user@example.com to a set of links. The Fediverse uses it to discover ActivityPub actors.
   https://specification.website/spec/well-known/webfinger/
4. Web Bot Auth — verifiable bot identity — optional · agent-readiness
   Web Bot Auth lets a bot prove who it is by signing each HTTP request with a key it controls. Sites can then allow or block specific bots without IP allow-lists, user-agent strings, or guesswork. Built on RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures.
   https://specification.website/spec/agent-readiness/web-bot-auth/
5. NLWeb — conversational interface discovery — optional · agent-readiness
   NLWeb is an emerging convention for exposing a site as a conversational AI endpoint. A site advertises an `/ask`-style endpoint via a `rel="nlweb"` link and serves an MCP-compatible JSON-RPC interface that agents can query in natural language.
   https://specification.website/spec/agent-readiness/nlweb/

# <meta name="description">
A short, unique summary of the page used by search engines and social platforms as a snippet. Google may rewrite it, but a good one is rewritten less often.
## What it is
A meta description is a short summary of the page, declared in <head> :
< meta name = "description" content = "The Website Specification is a platform-agnostic spec of what a good website must do, from doctype to security headers." />
The browser does not render it. It is metadata for crawlers, social platforms, and AI agents that fetch the page.
## Why it matters
The meta description does not directly affect search ranking, but it strongly affects whether the user clicks. Search engines often use it as the snippet shown beneath the title in results:
A good description that matches the user’s query gives them a reason to click.
A missing description forces the engine to invent one from the page body, which is often less compelling.
Google rewrites the description for about 70% of results, but matches the source more often when it is high quality.
Social platforms (Slack, Discord, iMessage, LinkedIn) use it as the preview text when no Open Graph description is set. AI agents and answer engines use it as a short canonical summary.
A description that is missing, duplicated across pages, or stuffed with keywords is a wasted asset on every result and every share.
## How to implement
Write one description per page, specific to that page:
120–160 characters is the sweet spot. Google typically truncates around 920 pixels on desktop, roughly 155–160 characters.
Front-load the unique value. Truncation eats the end.
Describe what the page is about, not the site. A reader skimming SERPs should be able to predict what they will find.
Plain language. No keyword lists, no marketing slogans, no all-caps.
One per page. Two pages with the same description is a duplicate-content signal.
<!-- Good --> < meta name = "description" content = "The lang attribute on < html> tells screen readers, browsers, and search engines what language the page is written in. Use a valid BCP 47 tag." /> <!-- Bad: too long, generic, no useful information --> < meta name = "description" content = "Welcome to our website. We are the best in the industry, providing world-class solutions for all your needs. Contact us today to learn more about what we do and how we can help your business grow in 2026." />
For the homepage, summarise the site as a whole. For article pages, summarise the article. For category or archive pages, describe what is in the category. Do not leave the description empty and do not auto-generate it from the first 160 characters of the body — that almost always picks up navigation or boilerplate.
If the page also sets <meta property="og:description"> , write each separately. Social platforms prefer the OG version; search engines prefer the plain meta description. They can be similar but rarely identical, because the audience and the truncation length differ.
## Common mistakes
Reusing the same description on every page (often pulled from a site-wide template field).
Stuffing keywords: “cheap shoes, buy shoes, shoes online, shoe shop”. Search engines ignore this and users distrust it.
Including the page title verbatim. The snippet shows both — repeating wastes space.
Going to 300+ characters. Anything past the truncation line is invisible.
Ending mid-sentence because the CMS truncates blindly. Write to fit.
## Verification
View source. <meta name="description" content="..."> must be in <head> and non-empty.
Run document.querySelector('meta[name="description"]').content in DevTools.
Crawl the site and check for duplicate descriptions. Any duplication is worth fixing.
Use a SERP preview tool to see how the snippet looks at the truncation length.

# <meta name="description">
A short, unique summary of the page used by search engines and social platforms as a snippet. Google may rewrite it, but a good one is rewritten less often.
## What it is
A meta description is a short summary of the page, declared in <head> :
< meta name = "description" content = "The Website Specification is a platform-agnostic spec of what a good website must do, from doctype to security headers." />
The browser does not render it. It is metadata for crawlers, social platforms, and AI agents that fetch the page.
## Why it matters
The meta description does not directly affect search ranking, but it strongly affects whether the user clicks. Search engines often use it as the snippet shown beneath the title in results:
A good description that matches the user’s query gives them a reason to click.
A missing description forces the engine to invent one from the page body, which is often less compelling.
Google rewrites the description for about 70% of results, but matches the source more often when it is high quality.
Social platforms (Slack, Discord, iMessage, LinkedIn) use it as the preview text when no Open Graph description is set. AI agents and answer engines use it as a short canonical summary.
A description that is missing, duplicated across pages, or stuffed with keywords is a wasted asset on every result and every share.
## How to implement
Write one description per page, specific to that page:
120–160 characters is the sweet spot. Google typically truncates around 920 pixels on desktop, roughly 155–160 characters.
Front-load the unique value. Truncation eats the end.
Describe what the page is about, not the site. A reader skimming SERPs should be able to predict what they will find.
Plain language. No keyword lists, no marketing slogans, no all-caps.
One per page. Two pages with the same description is a duplicate-content signal.
<!-- Good --> < meta name = "description" content = "The lang attribute on < html> tells screen readers, browsers, and search engines what language the page is written in. Use a valid BCP 47 tag." /> <!-- Bad: too long, generic, no useful information --> < meta name = "description" content = "Welcome to our website. We are the best in the industry, providing world-class solutions for all your needs. Contact us today to learn more about what we do and how we can help your business grow in 2026." />
For the homepage, summarise the site as a whole. For article pages, summarise the article. For category or archive pages, describe what is in the category. Do not leave the description empty and do not auto-generate it from the first 160 characters of the body — that almost always picks up navigation or boilerplate.
If the page also sets <meta property="og:description"> , write each separately. Social platforms prefer the OG version; search engines prefer the plain meta description. They can be similar but rarely identical, because the audience and the truncation length differ.
## Common mistakes
Reusing the same description on every page (often pulled from a site-wide template field).
Stuffing keywords: “cheap shoes, buy shoes, shoes online, shoe shop”. Search engines ignore this and users distrust it.
Including the page title verbatim. The snippet shows both — repeating wastes space.
Going to 300+ characters. Anything past the truncation line is invisible.
Ending mid-sentence because the CMS truncates blindly. Write to fit.
## Verification
View source. <meta name="description" content="..."> must be in <head> and non-empty.
Run document.querySelector('meta[name="description"]').content in DevTools.
Crawl the site and check for duplicate descriptions. Any duplication is worth fixing.
Use a SERP preview tool to see how the snippet looks at the truncation length.

# <meta name="description">
A short, unique summary of the page used by search engines and social platforms as a snippet. Google may rewrite it, but a good one is rewritten less often.
## What it is
A meta description is a short summary of the page, declared in <head> :
< meta name = "description" content = "The Website Specification is a platform-agnostic spec of what a good website must do, from doctype to security headers." />
The browser does not render it. It is metadata for crawlers, social platforms, and AI agents that fetch the page.
## Why it matters
The meta description does not directly affect search ranking, but it strongly affects whether the user clicks. Search engines often use it as the snippet shown beneath the title in results:
A good description that matches the user’s query gives them a reason to click.
A missing description forces the engine to invent one from the page body, which is often less compelling.
Google rewrites the description for about 70% of results, but matches the source more often when it is high quality.
Social platforms (Slack, Discord, iMessage, LinkedIn) use it as the preview text when no Open Graph description is set. AI agents and answer engines use it as a short canonical summary.
A description that is missing, duplicated across pages, or stuffed with keywords is a wasted asset on every result and every share.
## How to implement
Write one description per page, specific to that page:
120–160 characters is the sweet spot. Google typically truncates around 920 pixels on desktop, roughly 155–160 characters.
Front-load the unique value. Truncation eats the end.
Describe what the page is about, not the site. A reader skimming SERPs should be able to predict what they will find.
Plain language. No keyword lists, no marketing slogans, no all-caps.
One per page. Two pages with the same description is a duplicate-content signal.
<!-- Good --> < meta name = "description" content = "The lang attribute on < html> tells screen readers, browsers, and search engines what language the page is written in. Use a valid BCP 47 tag." /> <!-- Bad: too long, generic, no useful information --> < meta name = "description" content = "Welcome to our website. We are the best in the industry, providing world-class solutions for all your needs. Contact us today to learn more about what we do and how we can help your business grow in 2026." />
For the homepage, summarise the site as a whole. For article pages, summarise the article. For category or archive pages, describe what is in the category. Do not leave the description empty and do not auto-generate it from the first 160 characters of the body — that almost always picks up navigation or boilerplate.
If the page also sets <meta property="og:description"> , write each separately. Social platforms prefer the OG version; search engines prefer the plain meta description. They can be similar but rarely identical, because the audience and the truncation length differ.
## Common mistakes
Reusing the same description on every page (often pulled from a site-wide template field).
Stuffing keywords: “cheap shoes, buy shoes, shoes online, shoe shop”. Search engines ignore this and users distrust it.
Including the page title verbatim. The snippet shows both — repeating wastes space.
Going to 300+ characters. Anything past the truncation line is invisible.
Ending mid-sentence because the CMS truncates blindly. Write to fit.
## Verification
View source. <meta name="description" content="..."> must be in <head> and non-empty.
Run document.querySelector('meta[name="description"]').content in DevTools.
Crawl the site and check for duplicate descriptions. Any duplication is worth fixing.
Use a SERP preview tool to see how the snippet looks at the truncation length.

## What it is

A meta description is a short summary of the page, declared in `<head>`:

```html
<meta name="description" content="The Website Specification is a platform-agnostic spec of what a good website must do, from doctype to security headers." />
```

The browser does not render it. It is metadata for crawlers, social platforms, and AI agents that fetch the page.

## Why it matters

The meta description does not directly affect search ranking, but it strongly affects whether the user clicks. Search engines often use it as the snippet shown beneath the title in results:

- A good description that matches the user's query gives them a reason to click.
- A missing description forces the engine to invent one from the page body, which is often less compelling.
- Google rewrites the description for about 70% of results, but matches the source more often when it is high quality.

Social platforms (Slack, Discord, iMessage, LinkedIn) use it as the preview text when no Open Graph description is set. AI agents and answer engines use it as a short canonical summary.

A description that is missing, duplicated across pages, or stuffed with keywords is a wasted asset on every result and every share.

## How to implement

Write one description per page, specific to that page:

- **120–160 characters** is the sweet spot. Google typically truncates around 920 pixels on desktop, roughly 155–160 characters.
- **Front-load the unique value.** Truncation eats the end.
- **Describe what the page is about, not the site.** A reader skimming SERPs should be able to predict what they will find.
- **Plain language.** No keyword lists, no marketing slogans, no all-caps.
- **One per page.** Two pages with the same description is a duplicate-content signal.

```html
<!-- Good -->
<meta name="description" content="The lang attribute on <html> tells screen readers, browsers, and search engines what language the page is written in. Use a valid BCP 47 tag." />

<!-- Bad: too long, generic, no useful information -->
<meta name="description" content="Welcome to our website. We are the best in the industry, providing world-class solutions for all your needs. Contact us today to learn more about what we do and how we can help your business grow in 2026." />
```

For the homepage, summarise the site as a whole. For article pages, summarise the article. For category or archive pages, describe what is in the category. Do not leave the description empty and do not auto-generate it from the first 160 characters of the body — that almost always picks up navigation or boilerplate.

If the page also sets `<meta property="og:description">`, write each separately. Social platforms prefer the OG version; search engines prefer the plain meta description. They can be similar but rarely identical, because the audience and the truncation length differ.

## Common mistakes

- Reusing the same description on every page (often pulled from a site-wide template field).
- Stuffing keywords: "cheap shoes, buy shoes, shoes online, shoe shop". Search engines ignore this and users distrust it.
- Including the page title verbatim. The snippet shows both — repeating wastes space.
- Going to 300+ characters. Anything past the truncation line is invisible.
- Ending mid-sentence because the CMS truncates blindly. Write to fit.

## Verification

- View source. `<meta name="description" content="...">` must be in `<head>` and non-empty.
- Run `document.querySelector('meta[name="description"]').content` in DevTools.
- Crawl the site and check for duplicate descriptions. Any duplication is worth fixing.
- Use a SERP preview tool to see how the snippet looks at the truncation length.

# Touch target size
Interactive controls must be large enough to tap or click reliably. WCAG 2.2 sets a 24×24 CSS px minimum, with 44×44 CSS px as the enhanced target.
## What it is
A touch target is the area a user can tap, click, or otherwise activate to trigger a control — a button, a link, a checkbox, an icon. The target is not just the visible glyph; it is the full hit area the browser registers as activating the control.
WCAG 2.2 introduced a new Level AA success criterion, 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) , that requires interactive targets to be at least 24×24 CSS pixels . The older Level AAA criterion, 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced) , asks for 44×44 CSS pixels . Apple’s Human Interface Guidelines recommend 44pt , and Material Design recommends 48dp .
## Why it matters
Small targets are easy to miss. That penalises:
Users with motor impairments — Parkinson’s, tremors, arthritis, limited fine-motor control.
Users on small phones, or holding a phone one-handed on a commute.
Older users, whose pointing precision declines with age.
Anyone tapping while walking, in a moving vehicle, or wearing gloves.
Mis-taps are not just annoying. They can submit the wrong form, open the wrong link, or trigger destructive actions like “delete”.
## How to implement
Set a minimum size on every interactive element:
button , a .button , [ role = "button" ] { min-height : 44 px ; min-width : 44 px ; }
For icon-only buttons that must look small, expand the hit area with padding rather than shrinking the target:
.icon-button { display : inline-flex ; align-items : center ; justify-content : center ; min-height : 44 px ; min-width : 44 px ; padding : 10 px ; /* hit area extends past the 24px icon */ background : transparent ; border : 0 ; }
< button class = "icon-button" aria-label = "Close dialog" > < svg width = "24" height = "24" aria-hidden = "true" >…</ svg > </ button >
If a target genuinely must be smaller than 24 CSS px — for example, a dense data table — WCAG 2.5.8 allows it as long as a 24 px diameter circle around the target’s centre does not overlap any other target . The spacing alone satisfies the criterion.
Inline links inside running prose are exempt from both criteria. A link in a sentence is sized by the line-height of the paragraph, and forcing 44 px around each one would wreck typography.
## Adapt to the pointer
A mouse is precise; a fingertip is roughly 8–10 mm of imprecision. You can detect which the visitor is using and reserve the larger targets for touch, rather than forcing 44 px everywhere. The pointer and hover media features describe the primary input; any-pointer and any-hover describe whether any available input matches.
/* Touch / stylus as the primary pointer: enlarge tap targets. */ @media (pointer: coarse) { .toolbar button { min-height : 44 px ; min-width : 44 px ; } } /* No reliable hover (most touchscreens): don't hide controls behind :hover. */ @media ( hover : none) { .card-actions { opacity : 1 ; } }
Two cautions. Treat this as progressive enhancement on top of a baseline that is already accessible — 24 px is the floor for every pointer, so never use pointer: fine as an excuse to ship sub-24-px controls to mouse users. And remember many devices have both a touchscreen and a trackpad; when a control must work for the coarsest available input, test with any-pointer: coarse rather than pointer: coarse .
## Common mistakes
Setting font-size but no min-height on a button, so its hit area collapses on short labels.
Tiny close (×) icons in dialogs and toasts, 16 px or less, with no padding.
Stacking small icon buttons (share, like, bookmark) directly next to each other with no spacing.
Wrapping a small icon in a link without giving the <a> a block-level layout — the link only hits the glyph.
Removing padding “to make the design tighter” and shipping a button you can only tap with a stylus.
## Verification
Inspect the element in DevTools. Read the computed width and height (or the bounding box). Both must be at least 24 CSS px; aim for 44.
On a real phone, try tapping every primary control with a thumb, one-handed. If you miss, it is too small.
Run axe DevTools or Lighthouse — both flag WCAG 2.5.8 failures.
For dense UIs, draw a 24 px circle around each target’s centre and check no two circles overlap.

# Touch target size
Interactive controls must be large enough to tap or click reliably. WCAG 2.2 sets a 24×24 CSS px minimum, with 44×44 CSS px as the enhanced target.
## What it is
A touch target is the area a user can tap, click, or otherwise activate to trigger a control — a button, a link, a checkbox, an icon. The target is not just the visible glyph; it is the full hit area the browser registers as activating the control.
WCAG 2.2 introduced a new Level AA success criterion, 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) , that requires interactive targets to be at least 24×24 CSS pixels . The older Level AAA criterion, 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced) , asks for 44×44 CSS pixels . Apple’s Human Interface Guidelines recommend 44pt , and Material Design recommends 48dp .
## Why it matters
Small targets are easy to miss. That penalises:
Users with motor impairments — Parkinson’s, tremors, arthritis, limited fine-motor control.
Users on small phones, or holding a phone one-handed on a commute.
Older users, whose pointing precision declines with age.
Anyone tapping while walking, in a moving vehicle, or wearing gloves.
Mis-taps are not just annoying. They can submit the wrong form, open the wrong link, or trigger destructive actions like “delete”.
## How to implement
Set a minimum size on every interactive element:
button , a .button , [ role = "button" ] { min-height : 44 px ; min-width : 44 px ; }
For icon-only buttons that must look small, expand the hit area with padding rather than shrinking the target:
.icon-button { display : inline-flex ; align-items : center ; justify-content : center ; min-height : 44 px ; min-width : 44 px ; padding : 10 px ; /* hit area extends past the 24px icon */ background : transparent ; border : 0 ; }
< button class = "icon-button" aria-label = "Close dialog" > < svg width = "24" height = "24" aria-hidden = "true" >…</ svg > </ button >
If a target genuinely must be smaller than 24 CSS px — for example, a dense data table — WCAG 2.5.8 allows it as long as a 24 px diameter circle around the target’s centre does not overlap any other target . The spacing alone satisfies the criterion.
Inline links inside running prose are exempt from both criteria. A link in a sentence is sized by the line-height of the paragraph, and forcing 44 px around each one would wreck typography.
## Adapt to the pointer
A mouse is precise; a fingertip is roughly 8–10 mm of imprecision. You can detect which the visitor is using and reserve the larger targets for touch, rather than forcing 44 px everywhere. The pointer and hover media features describe the primary input; any-pointer and any-hover describe whether any available input matches.
/* Touch / stylus as the primary pointer: enlarge tap targets. */ @media (pointer: coarse) { .toolbar button { min-height : 44 px ; min-width : 44 px ; } } /* No reliable hover (most touchscreens): don't hide controls behind :hover. */ @media ( hover : none) { .card-actions { opacity : 1 ; } }
Two cautions. Treat this as progressive enhancement on top of a baseline that is already accessible — 24 px is the floor for every pointer, so never use pointer: fine as an excuse to ship sub-24-px controls to mouse users. And remember many devices have both a touchscreen and a trackpad; when a control must work for the coarsest available input, test with any-pointer: coarse rather than pointer: coarse .
## Common mistakes
Setting font-size but no min-height on a button, so its hit area collapses on short labels.
Tiny close (×) icons in dialogs and toasts, 16 px or less, with no padding.
Stacking small icon buttons (share, like, bookmark) directly next to each other with no spacing.
Wrapping a small icon in a link without giving the <a> a block-level layout — the link only hits the glyph.
Removing padding “to make the design tighter” and shipping a button you can only tap with a stylus.
## Verification
Inspect the element in DevTools. Read the computed width and height (or the bounding box). Both must be at least 24 CSS px; aim for 44.
On a real phone, try tapping every primary control with a thumb, one-handed. If you miss, it is too small.
Run axe DevTools or Lighthouse — both flag WCAG 2.5.8 failures.
For dense UIs, draw a 24 px circle around each target’s centre and check no two circles overlap.

## Why it matters

Small targets are easy to miss. That penalises:

- Users with motor impairments — Parkinson's, tremors, arthritis, limited fine-motor control.
- Users on small phones, or holding a phone one-handed on a commute.
- Older users, whose pointing precision declines with age.
- Anyone tapping while walking, in a moving vehicle, or wearing gloves.

Mis-taps are not just annoying. They can submit the wrong form, open the wrong link, or trigger destructive actions like "delete".

## How to implement

Set a minimum size on every interactive element:

```css
button,
a.button,
[role="button"] {
  min-height: 44px;
  min-width: 44px;
}
```

For icon-only buttons that must look small, expand the hit area with padding rather than shrinking the target:

```css
.icon-button {
  display: inline-flex;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: center;
  min-height: 44px;
  min-width: 44px;
  padding: 10px; /* hit area extends past the 24px icon */
  background: transparent;
  border: 0;
}
```

```html
<button class="icon-button" aria-label="Close dialog">
  <svg width="24" height="24" aria-hidden="true">…</svg>
</button>
```

If a target genuinely must be smaller than 24 CSS px — for example, a dense data table — WCAG 2.5.8 allows it as long as a **24 px diameter circle around the target's centre does not overlap any other target**. The spacing alone satisfies the criterion.

**Inline links inside running prose are exempt** from both criteria. A link in a sentence is sized by the line-height of the paragraph, and forcing 44 px around each one would wreck typography.

## Adapt to the pointer

A mouse is precise; a fingertip is roughly 8–10 mm of imprecision. You can detect which the visitor is using and reserve the larger targets for touch, rather than forcing 44 px everywhere. The `pointer` and `hover` media features describe the *primary* input; `any-pointer` and `any-hover` describe whether *any* available input matches.

```css
/* Touch / stylus as the primary pointer: enlarge tap targets. */
@media (pointer: coarse) {
  .toolbar button { min-height: 44px; min-width: 44px; }
}

/* No reliable hover (most touchscreens): don't hide controls behind :hover. */
@media (hover: none) {
  .card-actions { opacity: 1; }
}
```

Two cautions. Treat this as *progressive enhancement* on top of a baseline that is already accessible — 24 px is the floor for every pointer, so never use `pointer: fine` as an excuse to ship sub-24-px controls to mouse users. And remember many devices have both a touchscreen and a trackpad; when a control must work for the coarsest available input, test with `any-pointer: coarse` rather than `pointer: coarse`.

## Common mistakes

- Setting `font-size` but no `min-height` on a button, so its hit area collapses on short labels.
- Tiny close (×) icons in dialogs and toasts, 16 px or less, with no padding.
- Stacking small icon buttons (share, like, bookmark) directly next to each other with no spacing.
- Wrapping a small icon in a link without giving the `<a>` a block-level layout — the link only hits the glyph.
- Removing `padding` "to make the design tighter" and shipping a button you can only tap with a stylus.

## Verification

- Inspect the element in DevTools. Read the computed `width` and `height` (or the bounding box). Both must be at least 24 CSS px; aim for 44.
- On a real phone, try tapping every primary control with a thumb, one-handed. If you miss, it is too small.
- Run axe DevTools or Lighthouse — both flag WCAG 2.5.8 failures.
- For dense UIs, draw a 24 px circle around each target's centre and check no two circles overlap.

# Connections and tokens
Compare personal access tokens, internal connections, OAuth integrations, and public integrations for your Notion app or automation.

Choose a personal access token, internal connection, OAuth integration, or public integration based on who will use your app and how it needs to access Notion.
## ​Choose the right option
[62] link "Automate your own workUse a personal access token for scripts, tools, and Workers that run with your Notion permissions."
[63] link "Build a shared workspace toolUse an internal connection for tools your team shares, with access granted to the connection independently of any one person."
[64] link "Build an app for your workspacesUse an OAuth integration for internal tools where each person authorizes their own access. Your app acts on behalf of the user who connects it."
[65] link "Build an app for any workspaceUse a public integration so users in any workspace can authorize your app through OAuth. You can also apply to list it on the Marketplace."
## ​Compare the options
OAuth integrations and public integrations use the same OAuth authorization flow. Here, OAuth integrations are limited to selected workspaces, while public integrations are available to any workspace.

## ​Shared concepts
### ​Capabilities
[66] link "Capabilities" -> /reference/capabilities
determine which operations a connection or token can perform, such as reading pages, updating databases, or adding comments. Choose the capabilities your app needs.
### ​Content access
Capabilities and content access work together: permission to update pages does not grant access to every page. A personal access token uses your existing permissions. An internal connection needs content access granted to it. For OAuth integrations and public integrations, each user grants access during authorization. To share content:
Internal connections: Add the page or database in the Developer portal’s Content access tab, or open it in Notion and use Add connections . See
[67] link "Granting page access" -> /guides/connections-and-tokens/internal-connections#granting-page-access
for the steps.
OAuth integrations and public integrations: Each user selects pages in the OAuth page picker when authorizing the app. Selecting a parent page also grants access to its child pages. See
[68] link "Selecting pages during authorization" -> /guides/authorization/overview#select-pages-to-share
.
Personal access tokens: No separate sharing step is needed. The token uses its creator’s existing permissions, limited by its capabilities.
### ​Webhooks
Internal connections, OAuth integrations, and public integrations can subscribe to
[69] link "webhooks" -> /reference/webhooks
to respond to changes such as page updates and new comments. Use these when your app needs to react to changes without repeatedly checking the API.
## ​Getting started
Try the
[70] link "Quickstart" -> /guides/notion-api/quick-start
to create a page with a personal access token. For setup instructions and permissions, choose one of the guides above.
See
[71] link "Authorization" -> /guides/authorization/overview
for token authentication and OAuth flows, and
[72] link "API credential security" -> /guides/authorization/credential-security
for storing and protecting credentials.

For requests to pages, databases, and other workspace resources, send an Authorization: Bearer header with your token and a
[68] link "Notion-Version header" -> /reference/versioning

The object field identifies a resource, such as a page or user .
You can send page and database IDs with or without dashes.
Property names use snake_case .
Dates and timestamps use ISO 8601, such as 2026-03-11 or 2026-03-11T09:30:00.000Z .
To clear a
[71] link "URL page property" -> /reference/page-property-values#url

# Pagination
Read lists of results with cursor-based pagination in the Notion API.
[65] button "Copy page"

A paginated endpoint returns part of a list at a time. Read has_more to tell whether another page is available. A page can contain fewer items than you requested even when more remain.
## ​Requests
Parameter
Meaning
start_cursor
Omit it on the first request. For the next page, pass the previous response’s next_cursor unchanged.
page_size
The maximum number of items to return in one response. Most list endpoints default to 100 and accept values from 1 to 100.
For GET requests, pass these parameters in the query string. For
[67] link "search" -> /reference/post-search
and
[68] link "data source queries" -> /reference/query-a-data-source
, pass them in the POST body. Keep the same filters and sort order between requests.
## ​Responses
Field
Meaning
results
The items on this page of a standard list response.
has_more
true if another page of results is available.
next_cursor
The cursor for the next page, or null at the end of a standard list.
A standard list has object: "list" . Its type identifies the kind of result. For
[69] link "paginated page properties" -> /reference/property-item-object#paginated-values
, the response also includes information about the property.
[70] link "List data source templates" -> /reference/list-data-source-templates
returns items in templates . When you
[71] link "create a view query" -> /reference/create-view-query
, use its query_id with
[72] link "Get view query results" -> /reference/get-view-query-results

[73] link "block children" -> /reference/get-block-children
,
[74] link "users" -> /reference/get-users
,
[75] link "comments" -> /reference/list-comments
,

,

, and
[78] link "views" -> /reference/list-views
.

Set NOTION_API_KEY to your token and NOTION_BLOCK_ID to a page or block your token can read. The curl request requests up to two children. The JavaScript SDK example follows each cursor and prints one child ID at a time.

## Requests

| Parameter | Meaning |
| :- | :- |
| `start_cursor` | Omit it on the first request. For the next page, pass the previous response's `next_cursor` unchanged. |
| `page_size` | The maximum number of items to return in one response. Most list endpoints default to 100 and accept values from 1 to 100. |

For GET requests, pass these parameters in the query string. For [search](https://developers.notion.com/reference/post-search.md) and [data source queries](https://developers.notion.com/reference/query-a-data-source.md), pass them in the POST body. Keep the same filters and sort order between requests.

## Responses

| Field | Meaning |
| :- | :- |
| `results` | The items on this page of a standard list response. |
| `has_more` | `true` if another page of results is available. |
| `next_cursor` | The cursor for the next page, or `null` at the end of a standard list. |

A standard list has `object: "list"`. Its `type` identifies the kind of result. For [paginated page properties](https://developers.notion.com/reference/property-item-object.md#paginated-values), the response also includes information about the property.

[List data source templates](https://developers.notion.com/reference/list-data-source-templates.md) returns items in `templates`. When you [create a view query](https://developers.notion.com/reference/create-view-query.md), use its `query_id` with [Get view query results](https://developers.notion.com/reference/get-view-query-results.md) to read subsequent pages.

## Paginated endpoints

The endpoint reference gives the shape of each result. Common examples include [block children](https://developers.notion.com/reference/get-block-children.md), [users](https://developers.notion.com/reference/get-users.md), [comments](https://developers.notion.com/reference/list-comments.md), [file uploads](https://developers.notion.com/reference/list-file-uploads.md), [custom emojis](https://developers.notion.com/reference/list-custom-emojis.md), and [views](https://developers.notion.com/reference/list-views.md).

## Example

Set `NOTION_API_KEY` to your token and `NOTION_BLOCK_ID` to a page or block your token can read. The curl request requests up to two children. The JavaScript SDK example follows each cursor and prints one child ID at a time.

```bash curl theme={null}
curl --get "https://api.notion.com/v1/blocks/$NOTION_BLOCK_ID/children" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $NOTION_API_KEY" \
  -H "Notion-Version: 2026-03-11" \
  --data-urlencode "page_size=2"
```

```javascript JavaScript SDK theme={null}
import { Client, iteratePaginatedAPI } from "@notionhq/client";

const notion = new Client({ auth: process.env.NOTION_API_KEY });
for await (const block of iteratePaginatedAPI(notion.blocks.children.list, {
  block_id: process.env.NOTION_BLOCK_ID,
  page_size: 2,
})) {
  console.log(block.id);
}
```

For a large data source, a single query can reach its result limit even when `has_more` is false. See [Query large data sources](https://developers.notion.com/guides/data-apis/query-large-data-sources.md) to detect the limit and read the remaining rows.
